decisions.reason: The question asks what causes instability in learning systems with feedback loops and how much algorithmic interventions can reduce it without collecting more data.

Walker2d-v4 is the main example in the figure. The poster omits the offline one-step expert-action prediction setup, the deterministic Soft Actor Critic demonstrations in MuJoCo, and the 900-training and 100-validation trajectory split.

The figure labels reward and behavior cloning error separately. The poster omits the held-out one-step loss and 1,000-step closed-loop reward definitions, the mean over 20 fixed initial conditions, and the observation that reward can swing between consecutive updates while validation loss stays smooth.
The caption uses GVA without expanding it or explaining how unstable closed-loop dynamics amplify small parameter changes from minibatch gradient noise into large changes in long-horizon performance.

The method lists categories of interventions, and the figure compares architectures. The poster omits the persistence of oscillations with fresh independent expert trajectories and across standard regularizers, as well as the reductions from larger batches and aggressive learning-rate decay and their computational cost.

The figure compares raw and EMA curves, and the caption reports substantially reduced reward oscillations with the same batch size and learning-rate schedule. The poster does not spell out EMA or explain that it exponentially averages model parameters.
The poster omits the 270M-parameter TinyStories Transformer experiment, the switching-cost definition, its reduction with EMA, and its distinction from validation perplexity.

The poster omits TinyStories' role as a synthetic proxy, the preliminary English Wikipedia check, the interpretation of greedy completion agreement as stability, and the absence of a systematic generation-quality assessment.

The figure groups Ant and Humanoid as low-GVA tasks and shows the infrequent-update failure case. The caption recommends updating EMA at every iterate with an initial burn-in and a tuned averaging schedule.
